mcqs.question: Who proposed the term anaesthesia?
mcqs.explanation:
Oliver Wendell Holmes in 1846 was the first to propose the term anesthesia.
He used the term anesthesia to denote "the state that incorporates amnesia,
analgesia,
and
narcosis to make painless surgery possible"

Cocaine was the first topical anaesthetic and was discovered by Carl Koller in 1884.

First synthesized nitrous oxide.

William Morton:
Introduced ether anaesthesia.

mcqs.question: Passive euthanasia was recently made legal in which of the following countries?
mcqs.explanation:
Passive euthanasia is legal in India,
since 9 March 2018.
Prior to this,
it was legal only in
Netherlands,
Belgium,
and Luxembourg.
Euthanasia involves the administration of medication by someone o
ther than the patient for the
purpose
of ending the patient's life in the belief that it is best for the patient (but not necessarily at
the specific request of the patient).
Involuntary euthanasia,
which is done against the patient's consent,
is illegal in all countries and
amounts to murder.
Types of euthanasia:
•
Active euthanasia:
Direct administration of a lethal substance to the patient by another party
with merciful intent
•
Passive euthanasia:
Withholding or withdrawing o
f
life-sustaining treatment either at the
request of the patient or when prolonging life is considered futile
•
Indirect euthanasia:
Prescription of painkillers that may be fatal in an attempt to relieve
suffering
•
Physician-assisted suicide:
A medical professional aiding a patient in terminating their life upon
the patient's request

Which stage of spermatogenesis is characterized by an independent assortment of maternal
and paternal chromosomes?

measured as the rate of excretion of galactose in urine following the
ingestion or intravenous injection of a known amount of galactose.
Normally
,
l
ess than 3 g appear in the urine within 5 hours after the ingestion of 40 g of galactose.

mcqs.subject: Biochemistry
mcqs.chapter: Chemistry of Carbohydrates, Amino sugars and Mu...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common mucopolysaccharidosis?
mcqs.explanation:
The most common mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS)
is Sanfilippo disease (MPS III),
followed by
Hurler's disease and Hunter's disease.
Sanfilippo disease makes up a genetically heterogeneous but clinically similar group of 4
recognized types.
It is due to the deficiency of enzymes involved in the degradation of heparan
sulfate.
The onset of symptoms occurs between 2 and 6 years of age.
It is c
haracterized by severe CNS involvement with a mild somatic involvement.
Disproportionate
involvement
of CNS is a unique feature of MPS III.
Other features include sleep disturbances,
aggressive behavior problems,
and hirsutism.

mcqs.subject: Biochemistry
mcqs.chapter: Chemistry of Carbohydrates, Amino sugars and Mu...
mcqs.question:
A patient with deafness and mental retardation is found to have an excess accumulation of
glycosaminoglycans in his body.
After a detailed evaluation,
he is diagnosed with Hunter
disease.
What is the site of synthesis of these accumulated substances?
mcqs.explanation:
The sites of synthesis of glycosaminoglycans (GAG)
are the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi
apparatus.
Synthesis of the core proteins occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum,
whereas,
biosynthesis of
glycosaminoglycan chains and their subsequent m
odifications
occurs in the Golgi apparatus
Glycosaminoglycans or mucopolysaccharides are complex carbohydrates made up of amino sugars
and uronic acids.
They may be attached to a protein molecule to form a proteoglycan.
Proteoglycans are components of the ground substance of connective tissue.
Proteoglycans have a
bottle brush appearance.
Note:
Hyaluronic acid is the only GAG that is not synthesized by the Golgi apparatus.
It is formed
at the plasma membr
ane.
I
t participates in cellular migration among other things.

mcqs.subject: Biochemistry
mcqs.chapter: Chemistry of Carbohydrates, Amino sugars and Mu...
mcqs.question: What are the constituents of chondroitin sulfate?
mcqs.explanation:
Chondroitin sulfate is composed of N-acetyl galactosamine with sulfate and glucuronic acid.
Chondroitin sulfate is the most abundant GAG in the body.
It is located at sites of calcification in
endochondral bone,
cartilage,
tendons,
ligaments,
aorta,
and CNS.
In cartilages,
it binds collagen
and holds fibers in a tight,
strong network.15

mcqs.subject: Biochemistry
mcqs.chapter: Chemistry of Carbohydrates, Amino sugars and Mu...
mcqs.question: Which of the following mucopolysaccharides does not contain uronic acid?
mcqs.explanation:
Keratan sulfate is a mucopolysaccharide that does not contain uronic acid.
It is constituted by
repeating disaccharide units of N-acetyl glucosamine and galactose.
Two types of keratan sulfate are seen:
•
Keratan sulfate I - in the cornea
•
Keratan sulfate II - in the cartilage
It is present between the collagen fibrils in the cornea and plays a major role in corneal
transparency.
Hence,
its deficiency can lead to corneal opacity.

mcqs.subject: Biochemistry
mcqs.chapter: Chemistry of Carbohydrates, Amino sugars and Mu...
mcqs.question:
In a patient presenting with corneal opacity,
deficiency of which of the following could be a
likely cause?
mcqs.explanation:
Keratan sulfate I is present between the collagen fibrils in the cornea and plays a major role in
corneal
transparency.
Hence,
its deficiency can lead to corneal opacity.
Keratan sulfate is made of repeating units of N-acetyl glucosamine and galactose.
Two types of
keratan sulfate are seen:
•
Keratan sulfate I - in the cornea
•
Keratan sulfate II - in the cartilage
Dermatan sulfate (DS)
also plays a role in corneal transparency.
However,
DS is widely distributed
in the body,
mainly in the skin.

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the development of skin?

options.b: Expression of bone morphogenetic proteins by cells
options.c: Blocking of response to fibroblast growth factors
options.d: Lack of Wnt signalling promotes epidermal fate

mcqs.explanation:
Development of skin includes activation of Wnt signaling.
The lack of Wnt signaling promotes
the neural fate of the neuroectoderm cells
.
A single layer of neuroectoderm forms the nervous system or the skin epithelium depending on
the molecular signals it receives
.
Activation of Wnt signaling blocks the response of ectoderm
to fibroblast growth factors (FGFs)
and the cells express bone morphogenetic proteins
(BMPs).
This leads to the epidermal fate of the neuroectoderm
.13

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
Which layer of the epidermis is underdeveloped in the very low birth weight infants in the
initial 7 days?
mcqs.explanation:
Stratum corneum is underdeveloped in very low birth weight
(VLBW
)
infants in the initial 7 days.
In preterm infants,
the stratum corneum is permeable and becomes similar to the adult and
full
-term infant after 2-3 weeks of postnatal maturation.
The development of the layers of the epidermis starts from below upwards
.
Therefore,
the stratum
basale is the first to form and the stratum corneum is the last layer to form.

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
Choose the correctly labelled layer of the epidermis from the image given below
.
mcqs.explanation:
From superficial to deep
,
the layers of the epidermis are as marked in the image-
•
Stratum corneum
•
Stratum granulosum
•
Stratum spinosum
•
Stratum basale
The thick skin found in the palms and soles has an additional fifth layer,
called the stratum
lucidum
,
located between the stratum corneum and stratum granulosum.
The epidermis is made of superficial keratinized,
stratified
,
squamous epithelium
.
The epidermis
is a highly cellular layer but is avascular hence dependent on the underlying dermis for nutrition
via diffusion through the dermoepidermal junction.
It is thinnest on the eyelid and thickest on the palms and soles
.14

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
A patient presents with complaints of dry skin and lesions as shown.
The epidermal protein
deficient in this patient is present in:
mcqs.explanation:
The above image is suggestive of ichthyosis vulgaris which is due to the deficiency of filaggrin
protein.
They are found in the keratohyalin granules of stratum granulosum in the form of
profilaggrin (made of filaggrin monomers).
Profilaggrin undergoes proteolytic processing to yield individual filaggrin monomers that bind
and aggregate keratin bundles and intermediate filaments between the stratum granulosum and
corneum to form the epidermal barrier of the skin.

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
Which of the following are included in malpighian layer of the epidermis
?
mcqs.explanation:
The malpighian layer of the epidermis includes both stratum basale and stratum spinosum as a
unit.
It is named after Marcello Malpighi.15

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
Which of the following terms is used to describe the skin with all its appendages
?
mcqs.explanation:
Skin
,
hair,
nails,
the subcutaneous tissue below the skin,
and assorted glands constitute the
integumentary system
.
The most important function of the integumentary system is the
protection against external damage
.

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
Where are granules of Eleidin seen
?
mcqs.explanation:
Granules of Eleidin are clear intracellular proteins present in the stratum lucidum of the thick
skin of palms and soles
.
The cytoplasm of this layer is packed with keratin filaments and Eleidin granules giving it a
translucent appearance
.
It is also called the clear cell layer.

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question: Choose the incorrect statement regarding skin.

options.a:
Langerhans cells are dendritic cells which originate from bone marrow
.
options.b: Melanocytes are present in stratum basale.
options.c:
Stratified squamous epithelium with hallmark keratin filaments
.
options.d: Stratum lucidum is present between stratum spinosum and granulosum.

mcqs.explanation:
Stratum lucidum is the layer of the epidermis
,
which is present between the stratum corneum and
stratum granulosum.
It is present only in the thick skin of the palms and soles
.
It is also called
the clear cell layer due to the presence of refractile granules of Eleidin
.
The image below shows stratum lucidum sandwiched between stratum corneum above and
stratum granulosum below
.16

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
Which of the following layers of the skin predominantly contains non-nucleated cells
?
mcqs.explanation:
The stratum corneum,
also known as the horny layer,
consists of cells without the nucleus and
hence does not divide.
It prevents the entry of microbes from the environment into the body and prevents leakage of
fluids from the body to the environment.
This is called the barrier function.
As keratinocytes divide and move up to the stratum corneum from stratum basale,
they undergo
the following changes
:
•
Loss of nucleus and ability to divide
•
Increase in size
•
Change in shape and flattening
•
Dehydration and loss of water
•
Loss of metabolic activity
Note
:
In palmoplantar skin,
there is an additional zone,
also electron
\037lucent
,
the stratum
lucidum
,
which lies between the granulosum and corneum.
These cells are still nucleated and may
be referred to as transitional cells
.

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
Where are Odland bodies present
?
mcqs.explanation:
Odland bodies
,
lamellar bodies
,
or membrane-coating granules or keratinosomes are present in
the stratum granulosum and upper stratum spinosum.
They discharge lipid components into the intercellular space that plays an important role in
barrier function and intercellular cohesion
.17
The image below shows Odland bodies in stratum granulosum.
Green arrows indicate lamellar
granules in the cytoplasm
.
Red arrows indicate secreted lamellar granules.

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question: Melanocytes are present in which layer?
mcqs.explanation:
Melanocytes are present in the stratum basale (marking D).
These cells produce melanin which is packed into organelles called melanosomes and transferred
via finger-like processes called the dendrites to keratinocytes
.
Melanocytes originate from neural crest cells
.

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
Which of the following cells act as slow
-adapting touch receptors
?
mcqs.explanation:
18
Merkel cells
(Haascheiben cells
,
Merkel-Ranvier cells
,
or tactile epithelial cells
)
are oval-shaped
mechanoreceptors essential for light touch sensation and found in the skin of vertebrates
.
They are seen among the basal keratinocytes and contain desmosomes
.
They are abundant in the
highly sensitive areas of the skin like fingertips and synapse with somatosensory afferent nerve
fibers.
These cells may become malignant and form a Merkel cell carcinoma which is aggressive and
difficult to treat.

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
What is the location of Meissner
's corpuscle in the skin?
mcqs.explanation:
Meissner
's corpuscles are located in the skin just below the epidermis within the dermal papilla
.
They are concentrated predominantly over glabrous skin (non-hair bearing)
like fingertips and
lips.19

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
Which of the following are connected by desmosomes
?
mcqs.explanation:
Desmosomes connect keratinocytes in the epidermis of the skin.
Desmosome
(macula adherens
)
is a cell structure specialized for cell
-to-cell adhesion.
They resist
mechanical stress as they are strongly adhesive
.
Desmosomes contain proteins like desmoglein
(dsg
),
desmocollin
(dsc),
and desmoplakin (dp).
The loss of any one protein can lead to the separation of keratinocytes leading to acantholysis
.

mcqs.subject: Dermatology
mcqs.question:
A patient presents with multiple blisters on the skin and oral mucosa.
The
immunofluorescence staining for IgG shows the following characteristic pattern.
Which of the
following is targeted by the immune system in this condition?
mcqs.explanation:
The given image shows the characteristic fish-net pattern of immunofluorescence seen in
pemphigus vulgaris.
It is an autoimmune disease caused by antibodies directed
against desmoglein present in desmosomes
.
Loss of desmosomes results in loss of cohesion between keratinocytes
(acantholysis
)
and blister
formation.
Desmosomes failure can result in diseases of both skin and the heart.
Mutations within
the desmosomes are the main cause of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
(ARVC
).

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which embryological structure gives rise to the pinna?
mcqs.explanation:
The 1st and 2nd branchial arches give rise to the pinna (auricle)
through six mesenchymal
proliferation.
These proliferations are called auricular hillocks and they fuse to form the auricle.
The tissue from the second arch forms nearly all of the pinna.
The tissue from the first arch forms the tragus and external auditory meatus
.
Image showing the development of pinna:8

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question:
A patient is incidentally noted to have the following finding.
It is also present on the other
ear.
Which of the following is the cause for such abnormality?

options.a: Persistent opening of first branchial cleft

mcqs.explanation:
The given image showing the presence of sinus seen between the tragus and crus of the helix is
suggestive of the preauricular sinus.
It is due to improper fusion of the auricular tubercle formed
from the first and second arches.
The preauricular sinus is apparent at birth and is usually bilateral.
There may be occasional
sebaceous discharge from the punctum.
It does not regress spontaneously
.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question:
When are reconstructive surgeries for congenital malformations of pinna usually performed
?
mcqs.explanation:
Reconstructive surgeries for congenital malformations of the pinna (auricle)
are usually
performed around 5 or 6 years of age
.
Autologous cartilages from ribs are harvested for these
purposes and the ideal timing is between 6-10 years.
At around 3 years of age
,
85%
of the auricular growth is complete and the cartilaginous growth is
almost complete by 5 years.
Surgery performed on the auricle after 5 years doesn
't hinder further
growth
.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question:
Invagination of which of the following structures will form the external auditory meatus
?
mcqs.explanation:
Invagination of the first pharyngeal arch gives rise to the external auditory meatus
.
Previously,
it was believed that the external auditory meatus develops from the first pharyngeal
cleft
.
But recent studies suggest that the first pharyngeal arch gives rise to the external auditory
meatus
.9

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question:
Examination of a child with otorrhea revealed two discharging sinuses
.
One was present on
the floor of the left external auditory canal and the other on the left neck just below the angle
of the mandible.
Which of the following structures is abnormal here?
mcqs.explanation:
Given clinical scenario is suggestive of a collaural fistula
,
and the first branchial cleft is abnormal
here.
The fistula has two openings
:
•
One situated in the neck just below and behind the angle of mandible and
•
The other one in the external canal or the middle ear.
The track of the fistula traverses through the parotid in close relation to the facial nerve.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following structure develops from all three germ layers?
mcqs.explanation:
Tympanic membrane develops from all three germinal layers:
•
Outer epithelial layer is formed by the ectoderm
•
Inner mucosal layer by the endoderm
•
Middle fibrous layer by the mesoderm

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question:
Which of the structures given below forms the eustachian tube
?
mcqs.explanation:
The eustachian tube develops from the first pharyngeal pouch
.
Initially,
the first pharyngeal pouch forms the tubotympanic recess
.
The distal part of this recess
widens to form the middle ear cavity.
The proximal part forms the eustachian tube
.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following pharyngeal arches gives rise to malleus and incus?
mcqs.explanation:
The first pharyngeal arch gives rise to malleus and incus.
Stapes superstructure is formed from the second arch whereas the stapes footplate develops from
the otic capsule
.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question:
Which of the following arches gives rise to the stapes
?
mcqs.explanation:
The stapes develop from the second arch,
except for its footplate and annular ligament
,
which
develop from the otic capsule
.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following attains adult size before birth?
mcqs.explanation:
10
Ear ossicles attain adult size before birth.
The development of the middle ear:
•
The ossicles are full
-sized cartilage models by 15 weeks of gestation
.
•
Endochondral ossification is complete by 25 weeks
.
•
The middle ear is adult
-sized at birth.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following does not reach adult size at birth?
mcqs.explanation:
The mastoid does not reach adult size at birth.
It develops fully by 2 years of age
.
In infants and children up to 2 years of age
,
the mastoid process is not developed completely
.
So,
the facial nerve lies just beneath the skin near its exit.
Hence
,
during surgical procedures
,
the
incision is given slanting posteriorly
,
avoiding the lower part of the mastoid.
This spares the facial
nerve.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question:
An ENT surgeon has difficulty locating the mastoid antrum due to the presence of Korner's
septum
.
Which of the following sutures is persistent in this case?
mcqs.explanation:
The persistence of the petrosquamous suture is called Korner's septum and it is responsible for
the difficulty in locating the mastoid antrum and the deeper cells
.
Korner's septum separates superficial squamosal cells from the deep petrosal cells
.
Incomplete removal of disease at mastoidectomy can occur if Korner's septum is not
identified
.
Mastoid antrum cannot be reached unless the Korner's septum has been removed.
Below is an image showing Korner's septum
-11

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question:
From which of the following structure does the saccule develop
?
mcqs.explanation:
The saccule develops from pars inferior.
The development of the inner ear begins in the 3rd week of fetal life and is completed by the 16th
week.
The surface ectoderm on each side of the rhombencephalon thickens to form otic/auditory
placodes
,
which then invaginate to form the otic vesicle
(otocysts
).
The cells of the otic vesicle differentiate to form ganglion cells
,
which later develop into the
vestibulocochlear ganglia.
Later each otic vesicle divides into a dorsal component called pars
superior and a ventral component called pars inferior.
Pars superior gives rise to the utricle
,
semicircular canals,
and endolymphatic ducts
.
Pars inferior
gives rise to saccule and cochlear duct
.
The saccule is connected to the cochlea through a narrow
duct called ductus reuniens.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question:
From how many ossification centre
(s)
does the inner ear develop
?
mcqs.explanation:
The inner ear develops from 14 ossification centres
.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: When does the fetus start hearing?
mcqs.explanation:
The fetus starts hearing in the womb of the mother by 20 weeks of gestation due to sufficient
development of the cochlea
.12

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question:
A victim of child trafficking was brought to you by the police for age determination.
Which of
the following would you use as an accurate method for determining the same?
mcqs.explanation:
From the given options,
mineralization of teeth is the more accurate method of age determination
in childhood.
The relationship between the chronological age and dental age is stronger than between
chronological age and skeletal age.
Two aspects of tooth development have been used in the estimation of dental age:
•
The emergence of teeth -
superior part of the crown of the tooth appearing level with the surface
of the alveolar bone
•
The stage of mineralization of crowns and r
oots during development
Estimation
of dental age using mineralization stages of crowns and roots of developing teeth
includes visualization from a radiographic image.
This helps in viewing both erupted and
unerupted teeth.
It is a more accurate method of estimating age than emergence,
because
emergence is an event whose exact time of occurrence is not accurately known.
The study of dental microstructure is the most accurate method of age determination in
childhood
.
T
his involves counting perikymata (incremental lines on the surface of tooth enamel).
Note
:
Eruption is a continuous process by which a tooth moves from its crypt in the jaw bone to
its position of occlusion in the mouth.
It is different from emergence.
Emergence denotes that a
tooth has pierced the gingiva.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is the earliest tooth to erupt in a 7-month-old baby?
mcqs.explanation:
The earliest tooth to erupt in a 7-month-old baby (primary dentition)
is a mandibular central

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question:
Which o
f the following is a superadded permanent tooth?
mcqs.explanation:
The 6 molars are called superadded teeth.
Permanent dentition refers to the teeth which begin to erupt from 6th year of age and remain
throughout the life.
They are totally 32 in number.
The tooth distribution in each jaw is as follows:
•
4 incisors
•
2 canines
•
4 premolars11
•
6 molars.
Thus,
each jaw has 16 teeth.
Among these 4 incisors and 2 canines and 4 premolars are called as
successional teeth,
which erupt in the place of predecessor deciduous teeth.
The remaining 6 permanent molars (1st,
2nd,
and 3rd molar teeth)
erupt independently without
any predecessor teeth.
Hence they are called superadded teeth.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question:
Electron microscopy of the surface of tooth enamel revealed a neonatal line.
What is your
inference?
mcqs.explanation:
Neonatal line is an incremental line found on the surface of tooth enamel,
that indicates that an
infant was live born.
The study of dental microstructure,
which involves counting perikymata (incremental lines on the
surface of tooth enamel),
can provide an accurate method of age determination.
One particularly pronounced incremental line,
the neonatal line,
can be of medicolegal
significance in determining whether an infant was live-born or stillborn.
It is formed very s
oon
after
birth and can be visualized by light microscopy if the child survived for about 3 weeks or by
electron microscopy within 1 or 2 days of birth.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question:
A dentist evaluating a child's teeth notices the presence of mixed dentition.
What would be
the approximate age of the child?
mcqs.explanation:
6 – 12 years is the age of mixed dentition and the number of teeth remains constant at 24.
The period during which both primary and permanent teeth are in oral cavity together is known
as mixed dentition period.
This is the period where the deciduous teeth get replaced by
permanent successors.12

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question:
While examining the skeletal remains from a bomb blast,
a forensic expert decides to use the
Gustafson's method for identification of the ages of people killed.
Which of the following
would you not assess in this method?
mcqs.explanation:
Tooth length is not assessed in Gustafson's method.
Gustafson's method of estimation of age of an individual is based on physiological changes in
teeth.
It is mainly useful in adults over 25 years of age.
Gustafson's criteria includes:
•
Attrition -
wear and tear changes of occlusal surface
•
Periodontosis -
regression of gums surrounding the tooth resulting in loosening of the tooth and
falling
•
Secondary dentin -
deposition of dentin in pulp cavity
•
Cementum appositi
on - deposition o
f
cementum in the root forming incremental lines
•
Root resorption -
involves both cementum and dentin
•
Transparency of the root -
This is the most reliable criteria.
Canals in dentin get filled with
mineral and they become less transparent.
Gustafson's method has now been largely replaced by Lamendin's method.
Other methods of age determination based on teeth:
•
Lamendin's method
-
It evaluates root dentine translucency,
periodontopathy,
and tooth len
gth
•
M
iles
'
method
-
Uses transparency of the root as a single criterion
•
Boyd's method
-
Determination of age of an infant by counting incremental lines on enamel
•
Stack's method
-
Determination of age by measuring dimensions of teeth
•
Variation in racemization of amino acids (especially aspartic acid)
in dental pulp with age
•
Evaluating the reduction of the pulp chamber through X-rays

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question:
Which of the following is the most reliable criterion for age determination from Gustafson's
method?
mcqs.explanation:
Transparency of the root is the most reliable criterion in Gustafson's method.
Gustafson's m
ethod of estimation of age of an individual is based on physiological changes in
teeth
.
It is mainly useful in adults over 25 years of age.
Gustafson's criteria includes:
•
Attrition -
wear and tear changes of occlusal surface
•
Periodontosis -
regression of gums surrounding the tooth resulting in loosening of the tooth and
falling
•
Secondary dentin -
deposition of dentin in pulp cavity
•
Cementum apposition - deposition of cementum in the root forming incremental lines
•
R

involves both cementum and dentin13
•
Transparency of the root -
This is the most reliable criteria.
Canals in dentin get filled with
mineral and they become less transparent.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following methods is used for dental numbering?
mcqs.explanation:
Palmer's notation is used for charting of teeth.
Teeth will be numbered from 1 to 8 starting from
the central incisor till the third molar in each quadrant.
The image given below shows Palmer's notation for teeth charting.The 4 most commonly used methods in dental charting are:
1.
Universal system:
Teeth are numbered 1 – 16 starting from upper right to upper left and 17 – 32
starting from lower left to lower right.
The image given below shows the universal dental charting
system.14
2.
Palmer's notation:
Teeth will be numbered from 1 to 8 starting from the central incisor till the
third molar in each quadrant.
The image given below shows Palmer's notation for dental charting.3.
Haderup system:
This is similar to Palmer's notation but plus sign (+)
indicates upper teeth and
minus sign (-)
indicates lower teeth.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question:
Which of the following is the most reliable method for estimation of age in adulthood (>25
years)?
mcqs.explanation:
Estimation of age in adulthood
(>25 years)
is best estimated by degenerative changes in pubic
symphysis.
Physical anthropology has established several methods for determining age in adults which
include macroscopic,
microscopic,
and biomolecular methods.
Macroscopic methods of adult age determination are the most important ones and consist
principally in the degree of degeneration of selected articulations such as:
•
Pubic symphysis
•
Osteochondral surface o
f the 4th rib19
•
Auricular surface of the ilium
Suchey and Brooks described six phases of degenerative change in the pubic symphysis.
Until recently,
the most commonly used method for estimating age using the architecture of the
pubic symphysis was that of Todd,
who described 10 stages of pubic symphysis change during
aging.
More recently,
researchers Suchey and Brooks described six phases of degenerative change
in the pubic symphysis.
To solve this controversy,
the following is suggested:
A t
wo

•
If by looking at the skeleton,
the age of the individual seems to be within the first 3 phases of the
Suchey–Brookes pubic symphysis method,
then this should be the method of choice.
•
If the subject is classified in the last 3 phases,
then one should switch to the Lamendin technique
in order to assess age more accurately.
•
Currently,
age diagnosis at over 60 remains a problem.
In early adulthood,
Suchey-Brookes p
ubic symphysis method is most accurate.
In
late adulthood,
Lamendin technique of dental age estimation is most accurate.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question:
A soldier posted in Siachen is brought unconscious to the emergency ward.

,

?
mcqs.explanation:
In the given clinical scenario,
the rectal temperature would be the best site to measure the core
body temperature
.
At extremes of high or low temperatures
,
like in Siachen,
the axillary and the oral temperatures
are highly misleading and should not be used to measure the core body temperature
.
The infrared tympanic thermometer measures the temperature of the eardrum which is
representative of the core body temperature.
However,
it often ends up measuring the
temperature of the ear canal.
This is because of inadequate insertion into the ear canal due to

Hence
,

.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question:

mcqs.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of peritonitis

In renal colic,

Patients with meningitis present with neck stiffness
.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question:
What are petechiae
?

options.a: Large extravasation of blood in the skin

mcqs.explanation:
Petechiae are defined as skin hemorrhages appearing as minute non-blanching spots that measure
less than 2 mm.
A few conditions causing petechiae have been stated below
:
•
Infectious diseases
:
Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
infection
,
infective endocarditis
,
meningococcemia,
and viral hemorrhagic fevers.
•
Non-infectious conditions:
Vasculitis,
thrombocytopenia
,
leukemia,
scurvy,
and vitamin K
deficiency
•
Drugs:
Anticoagulants
(warfarin
,

.

mcqs.question:
A 28-year-old woman presented to the clinic with the lesions shown below
.
Which of the
following conditions is/are associated with this lesion?
mcqs.explanation:
The lesions shown in the image are spider naevi (nevus araneus).

•
Estrogen excess states such as pregnancy and OCP use18
•
Chronic liver disease
- especially alcoholic liver disease
•
Thyrotoxicosis
They are vascular lesions characterized by the tortuous dilatation of arterioles just underneath the
skin
.
On applying and releasing pressure over the lesion they typically fill from the centre
outward
.

mcqs.question:

.

,

.

•
Pulmonary
•
Bronchogenic carcinoma
•
Lung abscess
,
empyema
,
bronchiectasis

Interstitial lung diseases
•
Cystic fibrosis
•
Sarcoidosis
•
Asbestosis
•
GI

(Ulcerative colitis
,

)
•
Sprue
,
celiac disease
•
Neoplasms
- esophagus
,
liver,
bowel
•
Cirrhosis - juvenile and biliary
•
Chronic active hepatitis
•
Cardiovascular
•
Cyanotic congenital heart disease
•
Subacute bacterial endocarditis
•
Aortic aneurysm
•
Arteriovenous fistula
•
Patent ductus arteriosus with right to left shunt
•
Atrial myxoma
•
Endocrine

Grave's disease

•
CNS

Hemiplegia

)

Skin disease

Palmoplantar keratoderma

Malignancies

Thyroid cancer

Thymus cancer

mcqs.question:
A 40-year-old patient presents with loss of appetite
,

,
and easy bruisability.

mcqs.explanation:
The nail change seen in the given image is leukonychia totalis
.
It is a prominent feature of
hypoalbuminemic states
.
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of liver cirrhosis,
which leads to
hypoalbuminemia
.
Leukonychia is an opaque whitish discoloration of the nail and is seen in the following conditions:
•
Dietary deficiency
:
Protein-energy malnutrition,
pellagra
,
zinc deficiency
•
Drugs:
Cytotoxic agents
,
Steroids
,
Retinoids,
Pilocarpine
•
Dermatological pathology
:
Alopecia areata,
erythema multiforme
,
exfoliative dermatitis,
and SLE
•
Systemic diseases
:
Liver cirrhosis,

•
Miscellaneous
:
Trauma
,
malignancy,
and toxins (arsenic,

)
•
Idiopathic
Note
:

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question:
A resident is examining a patient with bilateral leg swelling below the knees.
He notes that on

,

.
What is the likely cause of the
edema
?
mcqs.explanation:
Bilateral non-pitting edema in the lower limbs is suggestive of myxedema
.
While chronic lymphangitis and acute lymphatic filariasis can also cause non-pitting edema
,
they
usually have a unilateral/localized presentation
.
Nephrotic syndrome and heart failure cause bilateral pitting edema
.
Causes of generalized edema include
:
•
Heart failure
•
Chronic renal failure
•
Nephrotic syndrome
•
Liver cirrhosis
Causes of localized edema include
:
•
Thrombophlebitis
•
Chronic lymphangitis
•
Resection of regional lymph nodes
•
Filariasis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question:
While examining a patient
's pulse
,
you note a tapping impulse when you raise his arm above
his head
.
Which of the following conditions would you not suspect in the patient
?
mcqs.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of water hammer pulse
,
which is not seen in left
-sided
heart failure.21
Collapsing pulse
/Watson's water hammer pulse is a rapidly rising pulse that collapses suddenly
.
This is because arterial pressure falls rapidly during late systole and diastole
.
It is also called
Corrigan
's pulse
.
The various causes of the collapsing pulse include
•
Physiologically,
it can be present in fever and pregnancy.
This is attributed to the combination of
increased cardiac output and the reduction in systemic vascular resistance
.
•
Cardiac lesions such as aortic regurgitation,
patent ductus arteriosus,
systolic hypertension
,
marked bradycardia,
aneurysm of sinus of Valsalva
•
High-output states such as anemia,
cor pulmonale
,
thyrotoxicosis
,
arteriovenous fistula
,
Paget
's
disease
,
beriberi,
and liver cirrhosis (secondary to chronic alcoholism)

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question:
True about the definition of Postural Hypotension
:

options.a: Decrease in Systolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 6 mins of standing
options.b: Decrease in Systolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 3 min of standing
options.c: Decrease in Diastolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 6 mins of standing
options.d: Decrease in diastolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 3 mins of standing

mcqs.explanation:
Orthostatic hypotension or postural hypotension is defined as a sustained drop in systolic BP of
\03720 mmHg or diastolic BP of
\03710 mmHg after 3 min of standing.
It can manifest as lightheadedness
/dizziness,
weakness or tiredness
,
difficulty
thinking/concentrating,
blurred vision,
and anxiety.
In non-neurogenic causes of orthostatic hypotension such as hypovolemia,
the drop in the blood
pressure is accompanied by a compensatory increase in heart rate of >15 beats
/min.
In
neurogenic causes
,
there is aggravation or precipitation of orthostatic hypotension by autonomic
stressors like a meal,
hot bath,
or exercise.
Non-neurogenic causes of orthostatic hypotension include
•
Cardiac pump failure - myocardial infarction,
myocarditis,
aortic stenosis
•
Hypovolemia - dehydration
,
diarrhea,
hemorrhage
•
Metabolic
- adrenocortical insufficiency
,
pheochromocytoma
•
Venous pooling
- sepsis
,
prolonged standing,
or recumbency
•
Medications
- alpha-blockers,
diuretics
,
phenothiazines
,
tricyclic antidepressants
Treatment includes removing reversible causes like drugs causing hypotension
.
Non-pharmacological interventions include patient education regarding staged moves from supine
to upright
,
raising the head of the bed
,
and increasing dietary fluid and salt.
If these fail,
drugs
like fludrocortisone and midodrine can be given.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question:
A 30-year-old African farmer presents with Winterbottom's sign.
This sign is due to the
involvement of:
mcqs.explanation:
Winterbottom's sign is due to the involvement of posterior cervical nodes
.

g
ambiense
/rhodesiense
.
It is transmitted through the bite of a Tsetse fly.22

maculopapular rash primarily involving the trunk.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Relative bradycardia occurs in:
mcqs.explanation:

,

and leptospirosis are infectious causes of relative

Relative bradycardia,
also known as Faget
's sign,
is observed when patients exhibit a lower heart

.
Body temperature is
commonly regarded as a factor that independently influences heart rate.
It is estimated that for
each 1\260C (1.8\260F)
rise in temperature
,
the heart rate typically increases by approximately 15-20
beats per minute.
While this pulse
-temperature dissociation is not highly sensitive or specific for establishing a
diagnosis,
it can still prove beneficial in resource
-limited settings due to its easy accessibility and
simplicity
.
Infectious causes of relative bradycardia include
:
•
Salmonella typhi
•
Francisella tularensis
•
Coxiella burnetii (Q fever)
•
Leptospira interrogans
•
Legionella pneumophila
•
Rickettsia spp
.
•
Orientia tsutsugamushi
(scrub typhus
)
•
Corynebacterium diphtheriae
•
Plasmodium spp
. (malaria
)
Noninfectious causes include
:
•
Drug fever
•
Beta-blocker use
•
Central nervous system lesions
•
Malignant lymphoma
•
Factitious fever

mcqs.question:
A patient with rheumatic heart disease now presents with fever and the following nail finding.

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of infective endocarditis
(IE).

.23

-red,

bed
.
Other peripheral manifestations of infective endocarditis include the following
:
•
Petechiae
:
Common but nonspecific finding
•
Purulent purpura
•
Osler nodes
:
Tender subcutaneous nodules usually found on the distal pads of the digits
•
Janeway lesions
:
Nontender maculae on the palms and soles
•
Roth spots
:
Relatively rare retinal hemorrhages with small,
clear centers

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Identify the condenser in the following image.
mcqs.explanation:
This is a modern compound microscope
,
and the condenser is located below the stage
.The purpose of the condenser lens is to focus the light from the illuminator onto the specimen
.
Microscopes with a stage condenser lens render a sharper image than those with no condenser
lens.
The simple microscope was invented first by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
,
the father of microscopy
and microbiology.
It uses 1 lens for magnification.
The compound microscope
,
introduced by
Hans and Zacharias Janssen uses 2 lenses
,
an objective lens and an eyepiece
,
to provide better
magnification power than the simple microscope
.

15
A painless genital ulcer with inguinal lymphadenopathy with the presence of spiral organisms on
microscopy is suggestive of syphilis
.

,
demonstrated
by dark
-field microscopy.
Dark
-field microscopy images have a dark background with a refractile organism.
The dark
ground microscope has an optical system that enhances the contrast of unstained bodies
.
It uses
reflected light and has a higher resolving power than the light microscope
.
Dark
-field microscopy
is the the most specific and sensitive technique to visualize Treponema pallidum when an active
chancre or condyloma lata is present

Other options
:
Option B:

.

dark image is formed on a light background.
Option C:

Mycobacterial species and malarial parasites
.

,
invented by Ernst Ruska,
helps in appreciating viral
structures
.

.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question:
Which among the following statements is false
?

options.a: Muramic acid is present in prokaryotes
options.b: Mitotic division is present in eukaryotes
options.d: Multiple linear chromosomes present in eukaryotes

mcqs.explanation:

mcqs.question: Which of the following methods will not help you visualize the bacterial cell wall?
mcqs.explanation:
The cell wall of bacteria cannot be seen with simple stains or direct light microscopy.16
The bacterial cell wall is present outside the plasma membrane and confers strength and shape to
the cell
.
It is composed of peptidoglycans.
The cell wall can be demonstrated by the following
methods
:
•
Plasmolysis
•
Microdissection
•
Reaction with specific antibodies
•
Mechanical rupture of the cell
•
Differential staining procedures
(E.g.
Chance's method
)
•
Electron microscopy
•
Fluorescence microscopy

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In which of the following phases of the bacterial growth curve does sporulation occur?
mcqs.explanation:
Sporulation occurs in the stationary phase of the bacterial growth curve,
which is marked as C in
the image.
The bacterial growth curve is obtained when a batch of bacteria is seeded in a liquid medium and
incubated
.
It consists of 4 distinct phases
:
•
Lag phase
(A) - The bacteria adapt to a new environment.
They synthesize and accumulate
enzymes and metabolic intermediates required for multiplication
.

(D) - Growth rate is negative

The population decreases due

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Pasteurization is done at ______.
mcqs.explanation:
Pasteurization is done at 63 degree Celsius for 30 minutes

Pasteurization is the process of applying heat to milk to kill or stunt the growth of pathogenic

vaccines for rabies and fowl cholera.

Transformation zone - the epithelium gradually changes from columnar to squamous in this
region.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
The newborn eye is usually
______.
mcqs.explanation:
A newborn is usually hypermetropic by +2D to +3D.
The anteroposterior (AP)
diameter of the eyeball at birth is about 16.5 mm,
which is about 70%
of
the adult size.
This reduced axial length causes light to converge behind the retina,
leading to12
hypermetropia
.
Additionally
,
the corneal diameter at birth is 10 mm.
The adult size (11.7 mm)
is attained by 2
years of age
.
The orbit is more divergent (50\260)
as compared to adult
(45\260).
Note
:
The lacrimal glands are underdeveloped in a newborn and,
hence
,
do not secrete tears.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
At what age would a child attain full visual acuity
?
mcqs.explanation:
Full visual acuity is attained by the age of 6 years.
Important milestones in visual development are:
•
At birth,
there is no central fixation,
and the eyes move randomly.
•
By the first month of life
,
the fixation reflex starts developing and becomes established by 6
months.
•
By 3 months,
binocular vision is established
.
•
By 6 months,
macular stereopsis and accommodation reflex are fully developed
.
•
By 6 years of age
,
full visual acuity
(6/6)
is attained
.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
A 45-year-old lady presents with the abnormality as shown below
.
She is diagnosed with uveal
melanoma.
What is the embryological origin of the cells involved?
mcqs.explanation:
Uveal melanomas arise from uveal melanocytes
.
Uveal and conjunctival melanocytes are derived
from the neural crest cells
.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
Which of the following statements is false regarding the development of the eye
?

options.a: The macula is fully developed at birth.
options.c: The cornea attains normal diameter by 2 years.
options.d:
Full visual acuity is attained by 6 years of age
.

mcqs.explanation:
The macula is fully developed by 4–6 months of age
.
Apart from the macula,
the rest of the retina
is fully developed at birth.
Postnatal Development of Eye
:
•
3 Months - Binocular single vision develops
.
•
4-6 Months - Macula fully develops
.
Fusional reflexes
,
stereopsis
,
and accommodation become
well developed
•
6 Months - Fixation,
which had started developing in the first month is now complete
•
2 Years - Cornea develops to the normal adult diameter
•
6 Years - Visual acuity fully develops and reaches 6/6
•
The lens,
however,
continues to grow throughout the life13

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: By how many weeks of embryonic development does the optic groove appear?
mcqs.explanation:
The optic groove appears by 3 weeks
.
By approximately day 22
,
2 small grooves appear on either
side of the developing forebrain in the neural folds
,
these are called optic grooves.
As the neural
tube closes
,
these grooves develop outpouchings called optic vesicles
.
These optic vesicles extend
from the forebrain to the surface ectoderm
.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Embryonic development of ciliary muscles is from _______.
mcqs.explanation: Embryonic development of ciliary muscles is from the neural crest.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
After conception
,
the canal of Schlemm appears by __________________ .
mcqs.explanation:
14
The canal of Schlemm appears by the 4th month after conception
.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
What is the anteroposterior diameter of the adult eyeball
?
mcqs.explanation:
The anteroposterior (AP)
diameter of the adult eye is 24 mm/2.4 cm.
At birth,
the average axial length of the eyeball is 16.5 mm.
By 3 years,
it grows rapidly to
approximately 23 mm.
From 3 to 14 years of age
,
the axial length gradually increases by a further
1 mm,
bringing it to the adult size of 24 mm.
This overall adjustment in the eye size,
including the
refractive power
,
is called emmetropization.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
A 34-year-old lady comes to the clinic complaining of problems in her vision.
On perimetry
,
a
visual field defect as shown below is obtained
.
Which of the following vessels does not supply
the anatomical location of the lesion?
mcqs.explanation:
The image shows bitemporal hemianopia,
a defect caused by optic chiasmal lesions
.
The
middle cerebral artery does not supply the optic chiasma.
Blood supply of optic chiasma:
•
Anterior cerebral artery - dorsal chiasma
•
Anterior communicating artery - ventral chiasma
•
Internal carotid artery - ventral chiasma
•
Superior hypophyseal artery - ventral (branch of internal carotid artery).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
A college student comes to the OPD for refractive error testing
.
Her eyes are dilated using
tropicamide.
Which of the following statements is false about the structure this drug acts on?

options.a:
It is triangular in cross section
.
options.b: There are around 30-40 processes in pars plana and pars plicata
options.c:
Its epithelium is derived from the anterior edge of the optic cup
.
options.d: The pars plana is approximately 4.5 mm from the limbus.

mcqs.explanation:
Tropicamide is a cycloplegic drug that acts on the ciliary body to cause mydriasis for refractory
error testing
.
The ciliary body is a triangular structure that contains 60-70 ciliary processes in15
each eye
,
present on the pars plicata.
The pars plana is 4.5mm from the limbus while the distance between the equator and the limbus
is 14mm
.
The ciliary epithelium is derived from the optic cup
(neuroectoderm
)
by the continued growth of
the outer lip's anterior edge
.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
A 12
-year-old girl you examined in an outreach camp is found to have this abnormality.
What
is the most common site where the condition is seen
?
mcqs.explanation:
The condition depicted in the image is a coloboma of the iris,
and the most common site of
coloboma is the inferonasal quadrant.
A coloboma is a congenital malformation in one of the structures in the eye
,
such as the iris,
retina,
choroid,
or optic disc,
due to the failure of embryonic fissure closure
.
Coloboma of the
uveal tract may be typical
(seen in the inferonasal quadrant
)
or atypical
(occasionally found in
other positions
).
Typical coloboma is of two types
:
•
Complete
:
Extends from pupil to optic nerve,
causing a corresponding lens indentation.
•
Incomplete
:
May involve iris alone,
or iris and ciliary body (more common),
or iris,
ciliary body
and a part of choroid.
Other embryonic remnants in the eye
:
•
Mittendorf
's dot - Remnant of the anterior end of the hyaloid artery
•
Bergmeister papilla
- Remnant of the posterior end of the hyaloid artery
•
Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous
(PHPV
) - Failure of fetal vasculature to regress
The image below shows a fundoscopy view of persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous.16

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
A child was brought with complaints of decreased vision.
Fundus examination shows a
developmental anomaly as shown below
.
What is the cause of this anomaly?

options.a: Incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure
options.b: Faulty migration of neural crest cells

mcqs.explanation:
The image shows a coloboma of the optic disc,
accompanied by a large chorioretinal coloboma
located below the optic disc,
which is caused by incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure
.
This developmental anomaly may involve the optic nerve,
choroid,
retina,
and iris.
Coloboma of
the optic disc can present in two forms:
a minor effect often associated with refractive errors like
hypermetropia and astigmatism and a fully developed coloboma that appears as a large
inferonasal whitish excavation resembling the optic disc.
Defective vision and superior visual field defects are typically associated with fully developed
coloboma.
Additionally
,
this condition may be associated with chorioretinal coloboma,
a
congenital anomaly where the developing optic cup fails to fuse completely
,
leading to abnormal
choroidal and retinal development
.
Note
:
Faulty migration of neural crest cells results in anterior segment dysgenesis
.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the embryological origin of the structure marked in the image?
mcqs.explanation:
The lacrimal gland arises from the surface ectoderm
.17

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
The optic foramen is situated between the
:

options.a: Lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid
options.b: Lesser wing and body of the sphenoid
options.c: Greater wing and body of the sphenoid
options.d: Two roots of the lesser wing of the sphenoid

mcqs.explanation:
The optic foramen is situated between the two roots of the lesser wing of the sphenoid
.
The optic foramen leads into the optic canal,
which is formed medially by the body and laterally
by the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone,
connecting the orbit's apex to the middle cranial fossa.
The optic canal transmits the optic nerve with its meningeal coverings;
the ophthalmic artery,
which is below the nerve,
is embedded in its dural sheath
,
and a few twigs from the sympathetic
plexus accompanying the artery.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question:
During a game,
a 26-year-old baseball player is hit in the head by a baseball
,
which fractures
the optic canal.
Which of the following pairs of structures is most likely to be damaged
?
mcqs.explanation:
18
In the given clinical scenario,
a fracture of the optic canal is most likely to damage the ophthalmic
artery and optic nerve,
as these are the primary structures passing through it.
The optic foramen leads into the optic canal,
which is a short cylindrical structure bounded
medially by the body and laterally by the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone,
connecting the orbit's
apex to the middle cranial fossa,
serving as a pathway for the aforementioned structures along
with its sympathetic plexus
.
Optic canal fractures,
often associated with basilar skull fractures,
can lead to optic neuropathy
.
The intracanalicular and intracranial portion of the optic nerve is most commonly affected in head
trauma.
Note
:
The greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bound the superior orbital fissure
.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a pathognomonic sign of a long bone fracture?
mcqs.explanation:
Abnormal mobility in a long bone is a pathognomonic sign of fracture.
A fracture is a break in the structural continuity of the bone.
Generally
,
movements occur in the
limb only at the joints.
If one is able to elicit mobility at locations other than the joints (say in the
middle of the arm
),
it is a definite sign of a fracture.
Crepitus may be felt while doing this.
Other
features of a fracture include
:
•
Pain13
•
Bruising
•
Swelling
•
Deformity
These can be due to a soft
-tissue injury or dislocation as well
.
Clinically,
eliciting abnormal movement or crepitus inflicts more pain.
Hence it is no longer
recommended.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: Match the following type of fractures with their associated mechanism of force.
mcqs.explanation:
The correct match is:
Most fractures occur due to a combination of forces
,
but the dominant mechanism of force is
revealed by the type of fracture.Type of fracture Mechanism of fo
rce
Transverse fractur
e
Tension
Oblique fracture Compression
Butterfly fragment Bending
Spiral fracture TwistingBased on the continuity of the periosteum
,
fractures can be complete or incomplete
.
In complete fractures,
the bone is split into two or more fragments and continuity of periosteum is
disrupted
.
It can be:14
•
Impacted fracture - The fracture fragments are jammed together and the fracture line is not
visible
•
Comminuted fracture - There is a fracture of more than two fragments
•
Segmental fracture - A separated fragment is seen in the middle
•
Avulsion fracture - Breaking of a piece of bone attached to a strong muscle
.
e.g.
olecranon and
patella fracture
In incomplete fractures,
the bone is incompletely split and the periosteum remains in continuity
.
They include:
•
Greenstick fractures:
The outer cortex breaks and the inner cortex bends causing the bone to
buckle like the snapping of a green twig.
It is seen in the pediatric population
.
•
Compression fractures:
Cancellous bone crumple due to force.
This is typically seen in vertebral
bodies
,
calcaneum,
and the tibial plateau.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question:
An elderly woman was brought to the OPD after she slipped and fell from her chair.
She is a
known case of breast cancer with distant metastasis
.
The X-ray of the patient is given below
.
Which of the following statements is false regarding this type of fracture?

options.b:
Mirels
'
score is used to assess the risk of fracture
options.c: FDG-PET or CT is the gold standard in evaluating bony metastasis
options.d: Pain occurs only after the fracture

mcqs.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with a history of trivial trauma,
breast cancer,
and the X-ray findings
are suggestive of a pathological fracture due to bone metastasis
.
Pain in the case of a pathological
fracture usually precedes the fracture.
Fractures occur due to:
•
Trauma
•
Repetitive stress
(stress or fatigue fracture)
•
Abnormal weakening of the bone (pathological fracture)
Pathological fractures are fractures that occur in a weakened bone that has structurally changed
due to some condition.
They occur either spontaneously or due to minor trauma.
The features
suggestive of a pathological fracture include
:
•
Pain at the site before the fracture
•
Multiple recent fractures
•
Elderly patient
•
History of primary malignancy
•
Unusual fracture pattern (Banana fracture - transverse fracture through an abnormal area of
bone,
similar to breaking a segment from a banana
)15
FDG-PET or CT is the gold standard in evaluating bony metastases
.
The risk of fracture in
metastatic bone lesions is assessed using Mirels'
score.
A Mirels's score >
8 warrants a prophylactic fixation.
Management of pathological fracture is
based on the causative lesion and survival of the patient
.Mirel's criteria

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question:
All of the following conditions can cause a pathological fracture,
except
:
mcqs.explanation:
Fabry's disease does not cause pathological fractures.
It presents with angiokeratomas and
acroparasthesias.
Pathological fractures are fractures that occur in a weakened bone that has structurally changed
due to some condition.
They occur either spontaneously or due to minor trauma.
In Gaucher's disease
,
there is a deficiency of glucocerebrosidase
.
This leads to an accumulation of
lipid-laden macrophages in the bone tissue
,
weakening the bone and causing fractures.
Osteogenesis imperfecta is an autosomal dominant disorder that occurs most commonly due to
mutation in the COL1A and COL2A genes
.
This results in the abnormal formation of type 1
collagen
.
Since type 1 collagen is mainly present in the bone,
the patient presents with repeated16
fractures with no or minimal trauma.
Hyperparathyroidism can cause severe bone resorption leading to bone pains and pathological
fracture.
Overall,
osteoporosis is the most common reason for pathological fractures.
Below the age of 20
,
the common causes of pathological fracture are benign bone tumors and cysts
.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question:
You are working as a medical officer in the Indian army.
An army recruit presents to you with
complaints of pain in the right foot.
He joined his training 6 months back.
His X-ray is given
below
.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing a fracture of the 2nd metatarsal are suggestive
of a March fracture.
It is a type of stress fracture.
Stress fractures (or fatigue fractures)
occur in a normal bone that is subjected to chronic repetitive
stress.
This initiates a bone remodeling process
.
When resorption occurs faster than replacement
,
the bone becomes liable to fracture.
Such fractures are typically seen in athletes
,
dancers,
or
military personnel who have a strenuous exercise regimen.
Common sites for stress fractures include
:
•
Metatarsals
(especially the second
,
march fracture)
•
Calcaneum
•
Navicular
•
Distal shaft of the fibula (runner's fracture)
•
Tibial shaft
•
Patella
•
Femoral neck
MRI is the investigation of choice to diagnose stress fractures.
It can visualize lower
-grade stress
injuries before X-ray changes appear.
A bone scan is the investigation of choice when multiple
sites have stress fractures.
Most stress fractures are managed using an elastic bandage and avoidance of painful activity until
the lesion heals
.
Stress fracture of the femoral neck should be managed by internal fixation as a
prophylactic measure
.
The image below shows a stress fracture:17

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions does the bone heal by increased callus formation?
mcqs.explanation:
Increased callus formation is seen with flexibly fixed fractures.
Fracture heals through direct union (primary bone healing)
or callus formation (secondary bone
healing).
•
Direct union:
This occurs when the fracture site is absolutely stable
.
This is seen in a fracture
held by a metal plate with absolute stability and in cases of impacted fracture in cancellous bones.
There is no stimulus for callus formation.
Osteoblastic new bone formation occurs directly
between the fracture fragments.
•
Callus formation:
This occurs when the fracture is not fixed rigidly.
The healing proceeds
through 5 stages
:
•
Hematoma formation
•
Inflammation
•
Soft callus formation
•
Hard callus formation
•
Remodeling
Healing by callus ensures mechanical strength as the movement and stress make the callus grow
stronger.18
The image below shows callus formation:

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question:
A teenager is brought to the casualty after sustaining a wrist injury during a sports meet
.
His
X-ray is given below
.
The orthopedic surgeon tries to reduce the fracture fragments by using
traction on soft tissues around the bones.
What is this technique known as?
mcqs.explanation:
The technique which uses traction on the soft tissue around the bones to reduce the fracture
fragments is known as ligamentotaxis
.
The given X-ray shows a fracture of the radial styloid
process
(Chauffeur
's fracture or Hutchinson fracture).
Reduction of the fracture is done to ensure normal alignment and adequate apposition of the bone
fragments.
There are two methods of reduction
:
•
Closed reduction
:
The fracture is reduced under appropriate anesthesia and muscle
relaxation.
Closed reduction of fracture relies on indirect fragment alignment utilizing the pull of
the soft tissue envelope
(ligaments and capsules
),
which is known as ligamentotaxis
.19
•
Open reduction
:
Operative reduction of the fracture under direct vision.
Option A and C:
Callotaxis is callus distraction or distraction osteogenesis
.
It is used for limb
lengthening or filling of large segmental defects in the bone.
Option D:
Arthrodesis (artificial ankylosis or syndesis
)
is the artificial induction of joint
ossification between two bones by surgery.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question:
Hanging cast is used to treat which of the following
?
mcqs.explanation:
A hanging cast is used to treat the fractured shaft of the humerus.
Humerus shaft fracture heals readily with just the external cast as it is usually enough to bring the
fragments into alignment.
The arm is placed over the lower chest with the elbow at 90\260.
A collar
and cuff support can be used to maintain the position.
The weight of the arm provides continuous
traction to the humerus (traction by gravity).After the fracture is reduced
,
it is important to hold the reduction with some restriction of
movements to promote soft
-tissue healing and to allow free movement of the unaffected
parts.
The methods of holding reduction include
:
•
Continuous traction (traction by gravity,
skin traction,
or skeletal traction)
•
Cast splintage
•
Functional bracing
•
Internal fixation
•
External fixation

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question:
A cast was applied to a patient with a wrist injury as shown below
.
What is this cast known
as?
mcqs.explanation:
20
The cast applied to a patient in the glass holding position is known as the scaphoid cast.
It is used
to treat scaphoid fractures.
To apply a scaphoid cast,
the wrist is held in slight dorsiflexion and the thumb is in abduction and
slight flexion as if the glass is being held between the index finger and thumb.
It extends from just
below the elbow to just proximal to the metacarpal necks of the digits
.
On the thumb,
the cast
extends just proximal to the interphalangeal joint.
Scaphoid fracture presents with pain and swelling over the radial aspect of the wrist.
A fall on an
outstretched hand could result in such a fracture.
The fracture can be confirmed (when an x-ray
does not show a fracture)
if there is pain elicited in the anatomical snuff box on the radial border
of the wrist.
An oblique x-ray of the wrist should be able to show a scaphoid fracture.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements are true about open fractures?
mcqs.explanation:
Open fractures are usually associated with multiple other injuries and compartment syndrome
can occur as a complication of open fractures.
Open fractures are characterized by a break in the overlying skin and soft tissues
.
Hence
,
the
fracture fragment is exposed to the external environment.
It is usually associated with multiple
other injuries.
The most common sites involved in open fractures include
•
Phalanges (Fingers and toes
)
•
Tibial diaphysis
•
Distal radius
•
Ankle
Open fractures are more prone to develop an infection
,
as it's exposed to the external
environment
.
The presence of an open fracture does not prevent the development of compartment
syndrome.
Major components of management of all open fractures are:
•
Antibiotic prophylaxis - It should be given as early as possible
•
Early debridement of the wound and fracture - This includes the following steps
:
•
Excision of the wound margins
•
Extension of the wound if required
•
Delivery of the fracture outside the wound for proper examination
•
Removal of the devitalized tissue
•
Cleansing of the wound to remove all the foreign materials
•
Nerves and tendons are usually left alone,
but if the wound is clean,
a repair can be considered
•
Wound cover
:21
•
In Gustilo Type I and II fractures wound cover can be done at the time of debridement
(Early
wound cover)
•
Delayed wound cover is usually practiced in Type III fractures
•
Fracture stabilization - The method of stabilization depends on the degree of contamination,
amount of soft tissue damage
,
and time from the injury to operation.
•
External fixation is used as a temporary measure if there is a delay in wound cover
•
If definitive wound cover can be achieved at the time of debridement and there is no significant
contamination,
then an open fracture can be managed as same as a closed injury

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question:
A 40-year-old man presents with a fracture of the right tibia following an RTA
.
On
examination
,
the wound is highly contaminated and appears as shown below
.
His distal
pulses are felt well
.
According to the Gustilo
-Anderson classification
,
this injury would be
classified as type
:
mcqs.explanation:
This open fracture will be classified as Type IIIB on Gustilo
-Anderson's classification due to the
extensive wound
(>10 cm),
high contamination,
very severe loss of soft tissue cover,
and intact
vascularity.
A fracture where the skin and soft tissues are breached is known as an open fracture (or
a compound fracture).
Gustilo and Anderson's classification is the most commonly followed
classification for open fractures.
Open fractures with an arterial injury that requires repair will be classified as IIIC
,
irrespective of
the size of the soft
-tissue wound
.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question:
You are the intern on duty and you receive patients who have been in a road traffic accident
.
For which of the following patients will you urgently call the orthopaedic resident on call?

options.b: Patient with a fractured arm with capillary refill time of less than 3 seconds in his fingers
options.c: Patient with a fractures arm with a 10 cm long incision over the arm
options.d: Patient with a fractured arm with capillary refill time of 5 seconds in his fingers

mcqs.explanation:
Capillary refill time of more than 3 seconds indicates inadequate limb perfusion
.
It is a surgical
emergency and could be due to either vascular injury by direct trauma or compartment
syndrome.
Hence an orthopedic intervention will be needed urgently
.
All other patients will also need an orthopedic intervention,
however,
the blood flow should be
restored at the earliest
.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question:
An industrial worker was rushed to casualty after he accidentally got his leg stuck in a
machine.
On examination,
he was found to have an open fracture as shown below
.
He was
urgently taken up for wound debridement and was considered for primary closure
.
It can be
performed in all of the following conditions,
except
:

options.a:
If injury to debridement interval <
12 hours
options.d: Wound margin can be closed without tension

mcqs.explanation:
When there is impaired nerve supply
,
primary closure of open fracture is not recommended
.
Primary closure of open fracture is the closure of the wound by direct skin suturing during the
index procedure (first debridement
).
In general
,
primary closure of wounds of Gustilo type I and
II fractures can be done at the time of debridement
.
In Gustilo type IIIA fractures,
some surgeons delay closure until a second
-look procedure is
performed.
In most cases of Gustilo type IIIB and IIIC injuries,
a delayed closure is practiced
.
Important criteria for primary closure
:
•
The patient
'
s
general condition should be stable22
•
Injury to debridement interval is <
12 hours
•
All necrotic material must have been removed
•
Stable fixation can be achieved either by internal or external fixation
•
Normal circulation
•
Intact nerve supply
•
The wound skin margins can be closed without tension
•
There should be no multisystem injuries

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question:
In which of the following fractures is surgical management necessary for optimum functional
results
?
mcqs.explanation:
Surgical management is necessary for optimum functional results in Monteggia fracture (fracture
of the ulnar shaft with concomitant dislocation of the radial head
).
While the other listed injuries may necessitate surgery in certain situations
,
conservative
treatment for Monteggia fracture yields poor results
.
Fractures in which surgical treatment will be needed to obtain an optimal result include
:
•
Displaced intraarticular fractures
•
Unstable fractures after failed conservative management
•
Major avulsion fractures after failed conservative management
•

mcqs.question: How many base pairs the human genome is made of?
mcqs.explanation:
The human genome is the complete set of nucleic acid sequences for humans and is made up of
3.2 billion base pairs.
It is encoded as DNA within the 23 chromosomes (haploid
).
In 2007,
a multinational project called Encyclopedia of DNA Elements
(ENCODE
)
concluded that
about 80%
of the human genome does not code for the proteins
.
However,
they allow for the
binding of proteins or are involved in the regulation of gene expression
,
in a cell type
-specific
fashion.
They are known as functional non-protein-coding genes
.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following describes the non-coding regulatory RNAs?

options.a: Transcribed from protein-coding regions of DNA and translated to regulatory proteins
options.b: Transcribed from protein-coding regions of DNA but never translated
options.c: Transcribed from non-protein-coding regions of DNA and translated to regulatory proteins
options.d: Transcribed from non-protein-coding regions of DNA but never translated

mcqs.explanation:
The non-coding regulatory RNAs are the functional non-protein-coding regions of the DNA,
which
are transcribed to RNA but are never translated into proteins
.
The two important types of non-coding regulatory RNAs are the micro RNA (miRNA
)
and the long
non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs).
These RNAs play an important role in the regulation of gene
expression
.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question:
What is the study of heritable changes in gene expression that are not caused by alterations in
DNA sequence?
mcqs.explanation:
Epigenetics is the branch of molecular biology that deals with the study of heritable changes in
gene function not involving changes in the DNA sequence
.
These heritable changes involve factors that mediate processes such as:
•
Histone organization
•
DNA methylation
•
Chromatin organization
These in turn regulate the genomic organization and gene expression in a cell
-type
-specific
fashion.
The dysregulation of these epigenomic factors plays a major role in the development of
malignancy.
Green tea catechins have been reported to modulate epigenetic processes
.
They can reverse DNA
methylation of tumor suppressor genes and increase the transcription of these genes
.13

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question:
Micro-RNA are involved during which of the following stages
?
mcqs.explanation:
Micro-RNAs (miRNA
)
act during the post
-transcriptional stage
.
It is a type of non-coding RNA.
The primary function of miRNA is to modulate the translation of
target mRNAs into their corresponding proteins
.
After the target RNA is transcribed from its gene
(post
-transcriptional),
the miRNA may either induce mRNA cleavage or repress its translation.
This is referred to as gene silencing
.
Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs)
are short RNA sequences that can be introduced experimentally
into cells
.
They have functions similar to endogenous miRNA
(serve as substrates for the Dicer
enzyme and interact with the RNA-induced silencing complex
).
They may have a therapeutic role
in silencing certain oncogenes
.

.

snoRNAs - involved in maturation of rRNA

assembly of ribosomes and noncoding RNAs
•

which modify histones and control gene
expression

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of cell injury?
mcqs.explanation:
Hypoxia is the most common cause of cell injury.
Causes of cell injury include
:
•
Hypoxia
•
Physical agents
•
Chemical agents and drugs
•
Infectious agents
•
Immunologic reactions
•
Genetic abnormalities14
•
Nutritional imbalances
The mechanism of hypoxic cell injury is reduced oxidative respiration.
The most common cause of
hypoxia is ischemia.
Hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1)
is a transcription factor with protective effects against hypoxic
injury such as:
•
Promotion of blood vessel formation
•
Stimulation of cell
-survival pathways
•
Enhancement of anaerobic glycolysis
The cells most sensitive to hypoxia are neurons.
The most sensitive neurons include
:
•
Pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus
(especially
,
area CA1,
also known as Sommer's sector
)
•
Cerebellar Purkinje cells
•
Pyramidal neurons in the cerebral cortex
The cells most resistant to hypoxia are fibroblasts.

options.b: Plasma membrane blebbing occurs in reversible cell injury

On removal of stimulus
,

mcqs.explanation:
On removal of stimulus
,

It is an irreversible cell injury.
Cellular adaptations are the reversible responses where the cells achieve an altered steady state in
response to physiologic or some pathologic stimuli.
They can be reversed if the stimulus causing
stress or injury is removed.
These cellular adaptations include
:
•
Hypertrophy
•
Hyperplasia
•
Atrophy
•
Metaplasia
Chronic sublethal stimuli are unable to cause cell death but may lead to certain changes in cells
,
such as:
•
Intracellular accumulations
•
Pathological calcifications
•
Cellular aging15

mcqs.question: Which among the following is not a feature of reversible cell injury?

options.a: Large amorphous densities in the mitochondria
options.d: Detachment of ribosomes from granular ER

mcqs.explanation:
Small amorphous densities are seen in the mitochondria in reversible cell injury.
The following changes occur in reversible cell injury:
•
Cellular swelling
- earliest change
•
ATP depletion leads to sodium-potassium pump failure
•
Na and water accumulate within the cell causing cellular swelling
•
Fatty change -
•
Seen in cells involved in or dependent on fat metabolism
(liver hepatocytes and myocardial cells
)
•
Light microscopy - no noticeable changes
•
Ultrastructural findings -
•
Mitochondrial swelling and small amorphous densities
•
Plasma membrane blebs
•
Swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum
(ER)
•
Detachment of ribosomes from granular ER
•
Nuclear changes like disaggregation of granular and fibrillar filaments
Note
:
The formation of large amorphous densities in the mitochondria is a feature of irreversible
injury.16

options.d: Nuclear changes like pyknosis and karyolysis

karyorrhexis,

•
Large amorphous floccular densities in mitochondria
•
Cell membrane blebs and loss of microvilli
•
Ribosomal detachment from endoplasmic reticulum

Thrombosis is is the formation of a blood clot inside a blood vessel

Stasis or turbulent blood flow
•
Hypercoagulability of the blood
