mcqs.question:
Which among the following do not usually undergo hyperplasia
?
mcqs.explanation:
Skeletal muscle and heart muscle usually undergo hypertrophy
,
not hyperplasia
.
Examples of physiologic hyperplasia
:
•
Female breast during puberty and pregnancy (hormonal hyperplasia
)
•
Uterine smooth muscle during early pregnancy
•
Compensatory hyperplasia of liver cells after partial resection
Examples of pathologic hyperplasia
:
•
Endometrial hyperplasia
•
Benign prostatic hyperplasia

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question: Which of the following timelines would be included in the perinatal period as per WHO?

options.a: 37th week of gestation to 28 days after birth
options.b: 20th week of gestation to 7 days after birth
options.c: 28th week of gestation to 28 days after birth
options.d: 22nd week of gestation to 7 days after birth

mcqs.explanation:
The WHO states that the perinatal period commences at 22 completed weeks and ends at seven
completed days after birth - 154 days.
It corresponds to when the fetus weighs 500g or more.
This definition is not to be confused with the period used for the calculation of the perinatal
mortality rate (PMR).
To calculate the PMR,
a fetal weight above 1000 g is considered
,
which is
achieved at 28 weeks of gestation
.
Therefore,
for all statistical purposes
,
international
comparisons,
and calculation of perinatal mortality rate,
the period from the 28th week of life is
considered
.10
Perinatal period
:
from the 22nd week
.
Perinatal mortality rate calculation:
from the 28th week
.
The neonatal period is defined as the first 28 days after birth.
Infancy is defined as the first
year of life
.
The image below shows various time periods
.
Only the time period for perinatal mortality and the
perinatal period are different as shown in the image.
For others,
corresponding mortality rates are
calculated using the same time periods shown.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
You would classify a baby as post
-term if it is born after ________
mcqs.explanation:
Post-term infants are those born after 42 completed weeks of gestation
,
as calculated from the
mother's last menstrual period
,
regardless of weight at birth.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
You would classify a baby as a very low birth weight baby if the weight of the baby is found to
be less than _____ kg.
mcqs.explanation:
A very low birth weight baby is one whose birth weight is <1.5 Kg
.
They are often premature
(<37 weeks of gestation
).
A low birth weight baby is one whose birth weight is <2.5 Kg
.
An extremely low birth weight baby is one whose birth weight is <1 kg.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
Reena,
a 34-year-old lady with gestation diabetes mellitus delivers an LGA baby at 37 weeks
.
What would the birth weight of this child be?
mcqs.explanation:
Infants with birth weight greater than the 90th percentile for their gestational age are called large
for gestational age
(LGA)
babies.11
Maternal diabetes and obesity are predisposing factors for LGA babies.
They have a higher
incidence of:
•
Birth injuries:
•
Brachial plexus injury
•
Phrenic nerve injury
•
Cephalohematomas
•
Hypoglycemia
•
Polycythemia
•
Congenital heart disease

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
As the intern assisting in the labor room,
you are tasked with administering Vitamin K to the
term newborns with no complications
.
Which of the following dose and route would you use
for administration?
mcqs.explanation:
All newborn infants are to be administered vitamin K at a dose of 0.5–1 mg intramuscularly,
to
prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (HDN).
However,
for newborns with vitamin K deficiency
,
the dose of vitamin K administered is 1–5 mg
intravenously.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
A term neonate born by normal vaginal delivery is diagnosed with hypothermia
.
Which of the
following is not a physiological response for heat regulation in this baby?

options.b: Breakdown of brown fat with noradrenaline secretion

mcqs.explanation:
Neonates do not generate heat by shivering.
Heat production in neonates happens by increasing the metabolic rate and oxygen consumption
by releasing norepinephrine
,
which results in non-shivering thermogenesis through
beta
-oxidation of brown fat.
This sympathetic surge also causes cutaneous vasoconstriction.12
Increased physical activity - crying,
increased body movements,
and muscular activity also
contribute to thermogenesis
.
Preterm and small-for-gestational
-age
(SGA)
infants have scanty brown fat stores
.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
You are conducting the routine newborn assessment of a 2.3 kg baby born 10 minutes back.
You would classify the neonate as having cold stress if you notice the body temperature to be:
mcqs.explanation:
A temperature of 36.0 to 36.4\260C categorizes a neonate as having cold stress
.
An infant's normal body temperature is 36.5 to 37.5 \260C.
It is measured in the apex of the baby's
axilla by holding the thermometer for at least 3 minutes
.
Hypothermia is an axillary temperature of <36.5 \260C.
•
Cold stress
:
36.0 to 36.4 \260C
•
Moderate hypothermia
:
32 to 35.9 \260C
•
Severe hypothermia
: <32 \260C
Hyperthermia is an axillary temperature of >37.5 \260C.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
A 24-year-old primigravida delivers a preterm baby at 33 weeks of gestation with a birth
weight of 2 kg.
She is advised to hold her child as shown below
.
Which of the following
statements about this method is false
?

options.b: Safety and thermal protection is equivalent to incubators
options.c: Reduces severe morbidity in the newborns
options.d: Should be performed only by the mother

mcqs.explanation:
Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC
)
can be carried out by the mother or any other caregiver.
KMC was introduced for the prevention of neonatal hypothermia in low birth weight
/
premature
newborns.
It has 4 components
—
•
Skin
-to-skin positioning of the newborn on the mother's chest
.
•
Adequate nutrition through breastfeeding
.
•
Early discharge and ambulatory care.
•
Support for mother and family for child care.
Evidence shows that-
•
It is as good as incubators,
in terms of safety and thermal protection
(measured by mortality)
•
Reduces severe morbidity by way of facilitating breastfeeding
•
Humanization of neonatal care
•
Promoted bonding between mother and child
Eligibility criteria for KMC
:
It is indicated for all hemodynamically stable low birth weight babies.
Short sessions of KMC can
be initiated in babies on medical treatment like IV fluids or oxygen therapy
.
Initiation of KMC can
vary with the birth weight of the baby.
•
Birth weight
<1200 g - It may take days to weeks for initiation of KMC
•
Birth weight
=1200
-1800 g - Only a few days may be taken before KMC initiation13
•
Birth weight
>1800 g - KMC can be initiated immediately after birth
All mothers without any serious illness can provide KMC
.
Positioning for KMC
:
The baby is placed between the mother's breast in an upright position.
The
hips are abducted and flexed in the frog position and the arms are also flexed
.
The abdomen of the
baby should be at the level of the mother's epigastrium
.
In this position,
the mother's breathing
would stimulate the baby and prevent the development of apnea.
The duration of KMC should be gradually increased from short sessions of more than one hour to
24 hours a day.
KMC is not necessary once the baby attains 2500 g of weight or 37 weeks of gestation
.
Note
:
Incubatory care,
feeding via nasal catheter
,
and prevention of infection are part of intensive care
for low birthweight babies.

mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
A 1.8 Kg neonate is born to a 24-year-old primigravida with no antenatal checkups
.
While
calculating the physical maturity of the neonate by the new Ballard scoring,
which of the
following criteria would you not take into account?
mcqs.explanation:
Palmar surface is not a component of the physical criteria for maturity according to the expanded
New Ballard score.

Lanugo

Eye

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
While examining a healthy term neonate
,
you notice that the baby passes greenish
-black
colored stools
.
This color is due to -
mcqs.explanation:
The greenish
-black color of the first stool in the newborn is due to biliverdin.
Meconium is a dark
,
sticky material that is normally present in the intestine at birth and passed in
the feces after birth.
It is detected in the ileum at about 70–85 days of fetal life and begins to fill
the colon and lower ileum late in the 4th month of gestation
.
The greenish color of the meconium
is the consequence of the bile pigments excreted by the biliary tract.
The main component16
responsible for the greenish color of the meconium is biliverdin (a pigment formed from the
oxidation of bilirubin).
Up to the 22nd week of gestation
,
the intestinal content is not greenish and for this reason,
fetal
defecation would not stain the amniotic fluid
.
The production of biliverdin starts over the next few
weeks or at a time closer to labor,
probably due to a biochemical switch related to the bilirubin
oxidation system
.
Bilirubin is responsible for the yellow color of the stools
.
Neonates do not harbor gut flora at birth.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
When does the parachute reflex disappear
?

options.c: At birth and reappears at 9 months

mcqs.explanation:
The parachute reflex has its onset at 7–8 months of age
.
It is fully developed by 10
-11 months of
age and remains throughout life
.
It can be evoked by holding the infant's trunk and then suddenly lowering the infant as if he or
she were falling.
The arms will spontaneously extend to break the infant's fall.
This reflex is a prerequisite to walking.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
A 6-day old infant is being examined.
While checking the reflexes
,
a brisk Moro's reflex is
noted
.
Which of the following conditions is a likely cause for this?
mcqs.explanation:
A brisk Moro reflex can be seen in neonates with hypoglycemia
.
In hypoglycemic babies,
there is an activation of the autonomic system
,
which results in
jitteriness
.
Newborns often exhibit this as an exaggerated Moro reflex
.
The Moro reflex is a primitive reflex that is very sensitive to the infant's level of alertness
.
It is
elicited by supporting the infant in the semierect position and allowing the infant's head to fall
backward onto the examiner's hand.
An animated gif of normal response to Moro's reflex where there is symmetrical extension and
abduction of the upper extremities
,
followed by flexion of the upper extremities is shown below17
The Moro reflex disappears by 6 months of age in normal infants.
Absent Moro reflex
:
caused by significant generalized disturbance of the CNS
•
Stage III HIE
•
Kernicterus
Asymmetric Moro reflex
:
feature of the root,
plexus
,
or nerve disease
•
Fractured clavicle
•
Brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy
)
•
Hemiparesis
Brisk Moro reflex
:
•
Neonatal hypoglycemia
•
Can also be a normal variant in healthy infants
•
Stage I HIE
Exaggerated
,
stereotyped
,
non-habituating Moro reflex is a feature of severe bilateral intrauterine
cerebral disturbance
,
perhaps because of the release of the brain stem from inhibitory cortical
influences
.
It is seen in conditions such as the following
:
•
Hydranencephaly
•
Severe micrencephaly
Moro reflex in different stages of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
(HIE):
•
Stage I HIE (mild):
Brisk
•
Stage II HIE (moderate
):
Weak/incomplete
•
Stage III HIE (severe):
Absent
Option A:
In kernicterus,
there is a deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia and
brain stem
.
Hence
,
the Moro reflex is absent
Option C:
In stage III HIE,
the muscles are flaccid and the infant is comatose
.
Thus,
the Moro
reflex is absent.
Option D:
Erb's palsy results from an injury to the brachial plexus
.
So,
the reflex is absent on the
side of injury as the nerve supplying the muscles involved (efferent of the reflex
)
is affected
.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question:
You are demonstrating findings in a pediatric OSCE examination on a 4-day old neonate
.
On
turning the baby's head to the left
,
you obtain the finding as shown below
.
At what age does
this reflex normally disappear
?
mcqs.explanation:
Asymmetric tonic neck reflex
(ATNR
)
disappears by 6 months postnatally
.
The tonic neck reflex is produced by manually rotating the infant's head to 1 side and observing
for the characteristic fencing posture
(extension of the arm on the side to which the face is rotated
and flexion of the contralateral arm
).18
An obligatory tonic neck response
,
in which the infant becomes
"stuck"
in the fencing posture
,
is
always abnormal and implies a CNS disorder.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question:
Fundoscopic evaluation in an HIV patient showed CMV retinitis.
He was started on
intravenous foscarnet,
a highly ionized drug.
Which of the following statements is true about
the drug?

options.b: Can cross the blood brain barrier easily

mcqs.explanation:
Highly ionized drugs like foscarnet are mainly excreted by the kidneys.
They are not reabsorbed from the renal tubules and are hence excreted unchanged by glomerular
filtration.
Dose reduction is necessary in renal impairment to avoid the accumulation of the drug
and associated toxicity
.
The non-ionized forms of weak acids and bases undergo tubular reabsorption.
Option B:
The blood-brain barrier limits the entry of ionized,
non-lipid soluble drugs.
Option C:
A drug is more readily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract when it is in its
unionized,
more lipophilic form.
Option D:
As the ionized form has low lipid solubility
,
it cannot penetrate cell membranes easily
.13

mcqs.question:

Alkalinization of the urine is done in barbiturate poisoning.
When the urine is alkaline,

When the tubular urine is made more alkaline,

acidification of urine increases the excretion of

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question:
When the pH = pKa of a drug,
which of the following statements is true?

options.a:
Concentration of the drug is 50%
ionic and 50 % non-ionic
options.b:
Concentration of the drug is 90%
ionic and 10
%
non-ionic
options.c:
Concentration of the drug is 75
%
ionic and 25 % non-ionic
options.d:
Concentration of the drug is 25%
ionic and 75
% non-ionic

mcqs.explanation:
When the pH = pKa of a drug,
the concentration of the drug is 50%
ionic and 50%
non-ionic.
pKa is defined as the pH at which a drug exists as 50%
ionized (hydrophilic
)
and 50%
unionized
(lipophilic
).
For e.g.,
phenobarbitone is an acidic drug with a pKa of 7.2.
At a pH of 7.2,
50%
will be unionized.
In a more basic plasma (pH=7.4),
a lesser fraction (around 40%)
will be unionized.
Small changes in pH near pKa of a drug may cause large variations in the degree of ionization.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question:
In a patient with nephrotic syndrome,
drug toxicity is least likely with which of the following
drugs?
mcqs.explanation:
In a patient with nephrotic syndrome,
drug toxicity is least likely with morphine.
Acidic drugs generally bind to plasma albumin while basic drugs bind to alpha-1 acid glycoprotein
.
Nephrotic syndrome reduces plasma albumin levels
,
therefore there is a decrease in the
protein-bound drug fraction and an increase in the free form,
resulting in drug toxicity
.
This is less likely with drugs having low plasma protein binding such as morphine (only around
35%).
Efavirenz,
diazepam,
and valproate have a very high plasma protein binding of >90%
and
predominantly bind to albumin and are associated with toxicity in hypoalbuminemia
.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question:
What does time for peak plasma concentration (Tmax
)
indicate
?
mcqs.explanation:
The time for peak plasma concentration (Tmax
)
indicates the rate at which the drug is absorbed
from the administered site
.
It depends on both the administered site and the drug formulation.14
This is used to determine the timing of the administration of hypnotics with respect to sleep
timings.
A hypnotic with a higher rate of absorption might be preferred to induce sleep at a
shorter latency as the target concentration can be achieved earlier.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question:
The pharmacokinetics of an experimental drug is being studied
.
If its apparent volume of
distribution is 6L
/kg,
which of the following is true regarding its distribution?
mcqs.explanation:
In the present case,
the volume of distribution of the drug is 6L
/kg (420 L in a normal adult with
reference weight 70kg)
which is very high when compared to the total body water of 42L
.
Therefore,
it can be implied that the drug is having high sequestration in tissues
.
The apparent volume of distribution (Vd)
is an imaginary volume throughout which
the drug is distributed if the plasma concentration remains constant throughout
.
Vd = Dose administered IV
/
plasma concentration
The difference in the volume of distribution based on drug type
:
•
Low Vd
•
Restricted to the intravascular compartment
•
Seen in drugs with high molecular weight
(e.g.,
heparin)
or high protein binding (e.g.,
warfarin
-
9.8L)
•
Medium Vd
•
Lipid insoluble drugs (e.g.,
gentamicin - 20L
)
do not enter the cells and are distributed in the
extracellular fluid volume
•
Small water-soluble molecules
(e.g.,
ethanol
- 42L
)
are distributed in the total body water
•
High Vd
•
Sequestered and accumulated in the tissues
•
Small lipophilic molecules
(e.g.,
chloroquine - 13000L
)

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question:
Which of the following parameters is used to assess the extent of drug absorption in a plasma
concentration vs.
time graph?
mcqs.explanation:
The area under the curve of plasma concentration vs.
time curve gives the extent of
absorption which is calculated by the trapezoidal rule.
The following image shows a plasma concentration vs.
time graph:15
Two drugs may have the same rate of absorption but a different extent of absorption or
bioavailability.
The factors upon which the extent of drug absorption depends are:
•
Lipophilicity
- If too lipophilic
(e.g.,
acyclovir),
the drug is not soluble enough to cross the water
layer adjacent to the cell
.
•
Hydrophilicity
- If too hydrophilic
(e.g.,
atenolol
),
the drug cannot cross the lipid cell membrane.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about first-order kinetics?

options.a: A constant amount of drug is eliminated in unit time
options.b: The half life increases with an increase in dose
options.c: The rate of elimination is constant
options.d: The rate of elimination is proportional to the plasma concentration

mcqs.explanation: The rate of elimination is proportional to plasma concentration in first-order kinetics.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: You would consider administering a loading dose for a patient if the drug has
mcqs.explanation:
The volume of distribution of the drug determines the loading dose of the drug.
Loading dose is a relatively large dose of the drug given initially to rapidly achieve the target
plasma concentration.
It is given by the formula
Loading Dose
= Vol.
of Distribution x Desired Steady
-state plasma Concentration.
The bioavailability determines the route of administration.
Though bioavailability may affect the
dose necessary,
it will not be the primary factor considered during the calculation of the loading
dose
.
Option A:
Clearance is used to determine the maintenance dose
.
Maintenance dose
= Clearance x Desired Steady
-state plasma concentration.
Options C and D:
Plasma half-life primarily determines the frequency of dosing.16

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question:
Which of the following drugs approach zero-order kinetics at higher therapeutic levels
?
mcqs.explanation:
Phenytoin kinetics changes from first-order to zero-order kinetics at higher therapeutic levels
.
True zero-order kinetics is shown only by ethanol
.
Some drugs have first-order kinetics at low plasma concentrations while at higher plasma
concentration (within therapeutic range
),
the mechanism for elimination gets saturated and they
change over to zero-order kinetics.
Drugs that show early saturation kinetics include
:
•
Warfarin
•
Aspirin
•
Theophylline
•
Verapamil
•
Fluoxetine
•
Phenytoin
Some drugs show zero-order kinetics at much higher (non-therapeutic
/ toxic)
levels
.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question:
Which of the following routes of administration will not bypass hepatic first-pass
metabolism
?
mcqs.explanation:
Hepatic first-pass metabolism occurs in drugs administered via the oral route.
When drugs are given orally,
they are absorbed in the intestine and reach the liver through the
portal vein.
During this process
,
the drug is acted on by enzymes of the liver and intestine
.
Additionally
,
the liver may excrete part of the drug in the bile,
further reducing the bioavailability.
This is called the first-pass metabolism
.
In all the other routes
,
the drug directly enters systemic circulation without reaching the liver.
Note
:
Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered dose of unchanged drug that reaches
the systemic circulation.
Hence
,
the bioavailability of a drug administered intravenously (I.V
)
is 100
%.
It is neither subjected to the first-pass metabolism as in the oral route nor does it depend
on local factors as in subcutaneous
,
intramuscular,
or transdermal.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question:
In the metabolism of xenobiotics
,
all of the following are phase 1 reactions except
?
mcqs.explanation:
Acetylation is a phase 2 reaction.
Metabolizing enzymes in hepatic cells
:
•
Microsomal enzymes
- present in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum
•
Non-microsomal enzymes
- present in mitochondria and cytoplasm17

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Sulphonamides undergo which of the following metabolic reactions?
mcqs.explanation:
Sulphonamides undergo acetylation
.
It is a phase II metabolic reaction where compounds having
amino or hydrazine residues are conjugated with the help of acetyl coenzyme
-A.
Drugs that undergo acetylation are:
•
Sulphonamides
•
Hydralazine
•
Isoniazid
•
PAS
•
Dapsone
•
Clonazepam
•
Procainamide

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question:
All of the following can cause lupus
-like syndromes except
:
mcqs.explanation:
Penicillin is not associated with a lupus
-like syndrome.
Drug-induced lupus is a consequence of genetic polymorphism of N-acetyl transferase 2 (NAT2
)
enzyme which results in slow acetylators and fast acetylators
:
•
Slow acetylators of isoniazid,
hydralazine,
and sulphonamides can have increased toxicity that
includes lupus
-like syndrome
•
Fast acetylators can have decreased efficacy as a result of faster metabolism of the active drug
Drugs that may result in lupus
-like syndrome (The SHIP MeChaniQ has lupus
-like syndrome)
are:
•
Sulphonamides
/
Sulfasalazine
•
Hydralazine
•
Isoniazid
•
Procainamide,
Para

The production of X-rays is as follows

Current is passed through a tungsten filament which acts as the cathode
\037
Electrons are emitted as a result of thermionic emission
\037
Electrons bombard the target anode,
a tungsten disc
\037
Results in the conversion of energy into heat
(99%)

The target anode is made of a tungsten disc in ordinary diagnostic X-ray tubes and molybdenum

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question:
The photoelectric effect can be best described as an interaction between
:

options.a: High energy incident photon and the inner shell electron
options.b: Low energy incident photon and the outer shell electron
options.c: High energy incident photon and the outer shell electron
options.d: Low energy incident photon and the inner shell electron

mcqs.explanation:
The photoelectric effect is an interaction between a low to intermediate energy X-ray beam and
the inner shell electron
.
When the inner shell electron is ejected
,
the outer electron goes into the inner orbit to occupy the
space
,
and the extra energy is ejected as characteristic radiation,
and is called the photoelectric
effect
.
The photoelectric effect is fundamentally important in diagnostic radiography since it is the
primary method by which contrast is developed in radiographs.
It allows for the differentiation of
different types of tissues on the X-ray film.11
Very low-energy X-rays are not capable of producing the photoelectric effect
.
High energy X-rays
are also not capable of photoelectric effect due to random scattering of electrons from the outer
shell
.
This is known as the Compton effect and it can lead to distortion of the image.
The goal of X-ray imaging should be to minimize the Compton effect and maximize the
photoelectric effect
.
The penetrating power of X-rays increases with increasing energy
,
which is
directly proportional to the frequency and inversely proportional to the wavelength
.

12

:
•

These patients can be managed

•
Net secretors
-

mcqs.question:
A patient with Crohn's disease has multiple skip lesions in the intestine
.
Surgical resection of
damaged areas is being planned
.
Removal of which part will cause steatorrhoea
?
mcqs.explanation:
Ileal resection may lead to steatorrhoea.
The ileum is the only site of absorption of vitamin B12 and bile salts.
Following resection of the
ileum
,
the loss of bile salts increases and is not met by an increase in synthesis
.
Depletion of the
bile salt pool results in fat malabsorption that presents with steatorrhea
.
The efficiency of water absorption in the jejunum is 44%
and in the is ileum 70%.
Resection of
ileum causes reduced conservation of fluid
.
Loss of bile salts into the colon affects colonic mucosa,
causing a reduction in salt and water absorption,
which increases stool losses
.
Small bowel motility is three times slower in the ileum than in the jejunum.
In addition,
the
ileocaecal valve may slow the transit.
Resection of the ileum results in a significant enhancement
of gastric motility and acceleration of intestinal transit.14

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question:
What is the best position for a conscious patient to be in during the insertion of a Ryle's tube
?
mcqs.explanation:
The best position for a conscious patient to be in during the insertion of Ryle's tube
(RT
)
is sitting
with neck flexion.
The described position helps in directing the RT towards the esophagus and
also prevents it from coiling in the oropharynx or entering the trachea.
RT
,
also known as nasogastric (NG)
tube
,
measures 120
-125 cm.
It has 4 markings at 40cm
(cardia),
50cm (body),
60cm (pylorus),
and 70 cm (duodenum
)
to indicate the approximate
position after the placement
.
Indications for NG tube
:
•
Feeding in patients with dysphagia
,
decreased appetite
,
or those who are nil per os (NPO)
for
medical or surgical reasons.
•
Aspiration of gastric fluid
•
Gastric decompression in cases of intestinal obstruction and paralytic ileus
.
•
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
•
Bowel irrigation
The absolute contraindications for an NG tube are severe midface trauma,
recent nasal surgery,
and basilar skull fractures15
Steps for the correct insertion of RT in an adult
:
•
Examination of the patient
's nostril for any anatomical abnormalities and then instillation with
10 ml of 1%
lignocaine
•
NEX method is used to measure the length of the RT
:
Place the exit port of the tube at the tip of
the nose.
Extend the tube to the earlobe,
and then to the xiphisternum.
•
The patient is asked to sit upright with partial neck flexion.
The tip of the Ryle's tube is
lubricated and passed along the floor of the nasal passage until a resistance is felt
(corresponds to
nasopharynx)
•
The patient is subsequently asked to swallow water to guide the tube through the esophagus into
the stomach until the marked length
(based on the NEX method
).
•
NG tube is finally taped to secure it in place
.
Confirmation of the correct position is done by:
•
Auscultation in the epigastric area while injecting a bolus of air
•
X-ray chest to locate the lead markers
•
Aspiration of contents and subsequently confirming gastric origin (pH <6 indicates gastric
placement
)
